result.summary: Æacus tells Cephalus how, after a plague emptied Ægina, he prayed to Jupiter for new citizens. Jupiter answered with thunder, and the ants of a sacred oak became men, the Myrmidons, who will follow Cephalus to war.

scenes.title: Prayer to Jupiter
scenes.summary: Stunned by the plague's devastation, Æacus prays to Jupiter to restore his people or bury him too. Jupiter sends lightning and thunder as a sign.
scenes.stakes: Æacus faces the total loss of his people and his kingdom, and is ready to die himself.

scenes.title: The Oak and the Ants
scenes.summary: Æacus sees ants streaming along the bark of Jupiter's oak and asks for as many citizens. The oak trembles without wind, and he hopes in secret.
scenes.stakes: Hope for a repopulated city hangs on whether Jupiter will answer.

scenes.title: The Dream of Men
scenes.summary: In a dream the ants fall from the oak, grow upright and take human shape. Æacus wakes and complains that the gods have not helped him.
scenes.stakes: Æacus risks despair, believing the vision false.

scenes.title: The Myrmidons Appear
scenes.summary: Telamon wakes his father to see the men in the palace, the same as in the dream. Æacus gives them the city and lands and names them Myrmidons.
scenes.stakes: The kingdom's survival depends on the new people being real.

scenes.title: Offer of Aid in War
scenes.summary: Æacus tells Cephalus the Myrmidons keep their ant-like thrift and will go with him to war once the wind changes.

notable_quotes.reason: Gives the origin of the Myrmidons' name from ants.

analysis.text: The passage shows renewal after catastrophe: divine favor, dreams and omens restore a people wiped out by plague.
It is an aetiological myth explaining the name Myrmidons, and a tale linking Ægina to Jupiter's oak oracle at Dodona.

legacy.text: The Myrmidons became proverbial for loyal, unquestioning followers; the word 'myrmidon' entered English with that sense.

fun_facts.text: Greek myrmex means 'ant', and the pun on Myrmidons is likely older than Ovid.

language_notes.text: Jupiter's union with Ægina, daughter of the river-god Asopus, produced Æacus. He appeals to this story to claim divine fatherhood and a father's duty.
'Propitious' means favorable. Thunder and lightning were read as signs of Jupiter's will, so the omen is taken as a yes.
Dodona in Epirus had the oldest oracle of Jupiter (Zeus), centered on a sacred oak. An oak grown from its acorns is therefore especially holy.
Myrmidons comes from the Greek myrmex, 'ant'. The name preserves their origin, as the sentence says.
The parenthesis explains Cephalus's arrival by east wind. He is waiting for a change to the south wind, which will allow the fleet to sail.

context_notes.text: Æacus, king of the island Ægina, is telling Cephalus how a plague sent by Juno emptied his island before the Myrmidons arrived.
Telamon is a son of Æacus and later father of Ajax. His arrival confirms the dream is real.

literary_notes.text: The ants' long train, heavy burdens and tiny mouths gives a vivid picture of orderly labor. This prepares for the later description of the Myrmidons' thrift.
He denies having hope yet admits he hoped. This shows the fear of a man who dares not trust a good omen after such losses.
The gradual change is described step by step: growth, standing upright, losing legs and dark color, taking human limbs. This makes the transformation seem vivid and almost natural.
The ants' habits are carried into the people, so a nation's character is explained by its origin. This is a typical aetiological touch.
